Lessons.Title: Scale Drawings
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Identify a valid scale drawing, distinguish uniform dilation from distortion, and dilate a polygon from a specified centre with a positive scale factor.

A scale drawing multiplies EVERY original length by one common positive scale factor k, so corresponding angles stay equal. Stretching only horizontal lengths by a different factor from vertical lengths generally distorts the figure and is not a scale drawing.

A dilation centred at P with factor k>0 sends A to A′ on ray PA with PA′=k·PA; if A=P, the centre stays fixed. The coordinate rule is A′=P+k(A−P). For 0<k<1 the image is closer to P; for k>1 farther away; k=1 identity.

Verbal diagram: centre P=(1,1) and triangle A=(3,1),B=(1,4),C=(3,4). A dilation by factor 2 gives A′=(5,1),B′=(1,7),C′=(5,7). Every original segment length is doubled and angle measures are preserved.

Original student task: distinguish two differently edited diagrams—one uniformly scaled, one stretched in one direction—by measuring two independent corresponding lengths. Then draw a dilation about a non-origin centre. Teacher rubric (0–8): correct centre/ray, a single consistent k, accurate measurements and a reasoned distortion test; actual hand drawings and critique require human scoring.
Source: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 3, CC BY 4.0. All diagrams are described verbally and all worked Edulytiks problems are independently authored.

1.1 Is That the Same Hippo? Source public-domain edited animal image contrasts one uniformly scaled copy and one distorted stretch. The original image is not included, so compare two independently drawn outline figures: one multiplies every pairwise distance by the same factor and keeps corresponding angles, the other expands width factor 2 and height factor 3 and is distorted. Learners describe two different lengths they would measure and a corresponding angle; do not infer scaling from one dimension alone.

1.2 Sketching Stretching: Source centre C and H at distance 40 mm, factor 3 yields CH-prime=120 mm, so original-to-image displacement HH-prime=80 mm (NOT 120 mm). With source factor 3/4 centre O, image K-prime lies on ray OK at OK-prime=(3/4)OK, not 3/4 of some other distance. Learners draw a ray from the named centre through the source point, then place the image the correct radius from centre, making both the centre and factor visible. Preserve source-specific misconception about measuring the wrong segment.

1.3 Mini Me: Source centre P for a figure with two circles, rays from P pass through each source control point (centres, endpoints and marked A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,I,J). Positive factor 1/2 locates every labelled image halfway along its own centre-to-point ray. It is insufficient to locate only D-prime and B-prime then guess other circles/vertices; every radius/segment must also shrink 1/2. Compare segment AB dilated about P and Q by the same factor 1/2: both image segments have length AB/2, although their positions differ. Even if Q tends arbitrarily far away, segment image length remains AB/2 for each finite Q.

Original independent Practice P1-P7: P1 source polygons P and Q scale ratio x=6 and unknown y requires teacher original figure, no fabricated numeric y; P2 given AB=6, CD=3, XY=4, ZW=a with AB↔XY and CD↔ZW yields a=2, equations 6/3=4/a and 6/4=3/a true; P3 equations 2/5=x/15 gives x=6, 4/3=x/7 gives x=28/3, 7/5=28/x gives x=20, 11/4=5/x gives x=20/11; P4 only rhombus necessarily has half-turn among given generic quadrilateral types; P5 prove rhombus diagonal reflection; P6 isosceles DAC and AB apex angle bisector implies AB perpendicular bisects CD by SAS; P7 parallel lines f,g equal-angle selections depend on missing original figure and require teacher review.

1.4 Publisher-locked Cool-down source not available. Independent Edulytiks paper equivalent asks to draw a centre-controlled factor-1/2 multi-point dilation, explain why different centres yield same output segment length while changing position, and reject a 2x horizontal 3x vertical distortion. Teacher human-scores four 0-2 dimensions.

KeyConcepts.Title: Scale factor
KeyConcepts.Definition: The ratio image length/original length shared by all corresponding lengths in a uniform scale copy.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use one positive factor for every segment.
KeyConcepts.Example: If an original side is 5 cm and its image is 15 cm, k=3.

KeyConcepts.Title: Positive-centre dilation
KeyConcepts.Definition: With centre P and factor k>0, P is fixed and every A lies on ray PA with PA′=k·PA.

KeyConcepts.Title: Distortion
KeyConcepts.Definition: A transformation that changes different lengths by inconsistent factors or alters corresponding angles.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check more than one independent side/ratio before calling an image scaled.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 2-by-3 rectangle changed to 4-by-9 has horizontal factor 2 and vertical factor 3, so it is not a uniform scale drawing.

WorkedExamples.Title: Dilate from a non-origin centre
WorkedExamples.Question: Dilate A=(3,1) about P=(1,1) by k=2.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use centre plus twice the displacement.
Steps: Check PA=2 and PA′=4 so PA′/PA=2.
WorkedExamples.Check: The image lies on the same ray from P through A, not on the opposite ray.

WorkedExamples.Title: Test a distorted rectangle
WorkedExamples.Question: Original rectangle is 2 cm wide and 3 cm tall; an edited image is 4 cm wide and 9 cm tall. Is it a scale copy?
Steps: A uniform dilation requires both ratios to equal one factor k.
Since 2≠3, no single uniform scale factor exists.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No, the edited rectangle is distorted.
WorkedExamples.Check: Independent sides suffice to disprove uniformity; a matching single side would not.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reduce a triangle
WorkedExamples.Question: A segment is 12 mm from the dilation centre. Where does its point image lie with k=3/4?
WorkedExamples.Method: Multiply the centre-to-point distance while staying on its ray.
Steps: Positive factor k=3/4 is less than 1, so the point moves toward the centre.
Mark A′ on ray PA between P and A at 9 mm from P.
WorkedExamples.Answer: A′ is 9 mm from the centre on ray PA.
WorkedExamples.Check: The image lies between the centre and original point because 0<k<1.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Scaling x and y coordinates from the origin when the specified centre is elsewhere.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: This changes the centre-to-point rays and gives wrong locations.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Subtract the actual centre, multiply the displacement, then add the centre back.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating unequal width and height factors as a valid scale copy.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It distorts angles and segment ratios.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Verify one common positive ratio for independent corresponding lengths.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating displacement HH-prime as 120 mm when the radius from centre C to image H-prime should equal 120 mm.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Source CH=40, dilation k=3: CH-prime=120 but HH-prime=80 on same ray.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Measure every image from the correct centre, not from its original point; compare centre-to-image and centre-to-original lengths.

SummaryPoints: Uniform scale drawings multiply all lengths by one positive k and preserve angles.
A dilation needs an explicit centre and scales centre-to-point distances along rays.
Hand-drawn scale figures and distortion arguments are teacher scored, not certified by one numeric response.

Lessons.Title: Scale of the Solar System
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Use proportional reasoning to model very different astronomical distances and diameters at one consistent scale, interpret feasibility limits, and estimate how a model of aligned objects affects apparent angular size.

This is an optional source modelling lesson. Astronomical values may be rounded; each real-world value must be declared as a modelling estimate rather than claimed exact. One scale must apply to BOTH diameters and distances if the representation is genuinely to scale.

Model assumptions: take Earth's diameter to be approximately 12,700 km and the Earth–Sun distance approximately 150,000,000 km. If Earth's diameter is represented by a 2 cm model circle, the Sun's scaled separation is (150,000,000/12,700)·2 cm≈23,622 cm≈236.2 m. That size is far beyond a classroom; do not secretly shorten distances while keeping object diameters on the same alleged scale.

For an idealized apparent-size comparison, if two objects are small relative to their distance from the observer, angular diameter is approximately diameter/distance in radians. Equal apparent diameters are modelled by equal such quotients; eclipses also require line-of-sight alignment. The simple ratio is an approximation, not a proof about real eclipse timings or orbital geometry.

Original task: design a scale-model proposal with exact written scale and rounded source measurements, then identify which proposed classroom placements cannot fit and why. Discuss relative diameters versus centre-to-centre distances. Teacher rubric (0–4): single consistent scale, unit conversion, reasonable rounding and physical limitations; model presentation and written critique are human assessed.
Source: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 3, CC BY 4.0. All diagrams are described verbally and all worked Edulytiks problems are independently authored.

KeyConcepts.Title: Single scale for unlike quantities
KeyConcepts.Definition: One proportional conversion applied to all lengths, including diameters, radii and distances.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Convert units before comparing model-to-real ratios.
KeyConcepts.Example: Earth diameter ≈12,700 km to 2 cm fixes 1 cm as approximately 6,350 km in the model.

KeyConcepts.Title: Magnitude and feasibility
KeyConcepts.Definition: A mathematically correct scale can yield a model much larger than available physical space.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compute needed dimensions rather than assuming everything fits on a page.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 2-cm Earth needs approximately 236 m separation from Sun at the stated rounded scale.

KeyConcepts.Title: Angular size approximation
KeyConcepts.Definition: For a small angular diameter, apparent size is approximately the object's diameter divided by its distance from an observer.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use equal diameter/distance quotients only for approximately equal angular size and state alignment assumptions.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 1000-km disc at 1,000,000 km and a 2-km disc at 2000 km both subtend ≈0.001 radians.

WorkedExamples.Title: Scaled Earth–Sun separation
WorkedExamples.Question: With estimated Earth diameter 12,700 km and Sun separation 150,000,000 km, how far apart are scaled centres when Earth is 2 cm across?
Steps: Multiply real distance: (150,000,000 km)·(2 cm/12,700 km)≈23,622 cm.
Convert centimetres to metres by dividing 100: about 236.2 m.
Compare with actual room dimensions and report the physical feasibility limitation.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Approximately 236 m of model separation, so a classroom model cannot maintain both sizes and distances at that scale.
WorkedExamples.Check: Unit km cancels and 23,622 cm≈236.22 m; using kilometres directly as centimetres would be wrong.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare approximate apparent sizes
WorkedExamples.Question: Hypothetical disc A is 1000 km across at 1,000,000 km; disc B is 2 km across at 2000 km. Are apparent diameters approximately equal?
Steps: The quotients agree, giving nearly equal small angular diameters.
This alone does not ensure an eclipse: the discs must also be aligned from the observer.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Yes, their small-angle apparent diameters are approximately equal.
WorkedExamples.Check: The approximation is valid because both ratios are small (0.001).

WorkedExamples.Title: Convert diameter scaling to another body
WorkedExamples.Question: Suppose a hypothetical planet diameter is 50,800 km at the same model scale as 12,700-km Earth shown as 2 cm. What is the model diameter?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the ratio of real diameters.
Steps: Multiply Earth model diameter 2 cm by 4.
New planet model diameter is 8 cm.
The centre separation must be calculated from actual distance data using the same scale, not invented from this diameter.
WorkedExamples.Check: This is a hypothetical planet, not a claim about a named planet's measured physical diameter.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Applying one scale to planet sizes and a different unstated scale to their distances.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The resulting drawing cannot honestly be described as one scale model.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Declare separate illustrative scales explicitly if needed; otherwise use one scale for every length.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Confusing angular-size equality with actual eclipse occurrence.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: An eclipse also requires suitable alignment and time-dependent positions.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Treat diameter/distance as an approximate apparent-size condition, and list the missing geometric/orbital conditions.

SummaryPoints: A single scale controls all physical lengths, which can make astronomical models impractically large.
Proportional calculations must preserve units and distinguish rounded estimates from exact measurements.
Apparent size is approximately diameter divided by distance in the small-angle regime; authentic modelling needs teacher review.

Lessons.Title: Measuring Dilations
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Measure and compare centre-to-point distances and corresponding polygon lengths under positive dilations, and explain why each ratio equals the same scale factor k.

A dilation with centre O and k>0 takes P to P′ satisfying OP′=k·OP on ray OP. This equality of distances from the centre follows directly from the definition. For other pairwise lengths, the constant-ratio property can be checked by measurement and coordinate reasoning; every corresponding length changes by factor k.

Verbal diagram: O=(1,1), original triangle A=(2,1), B=(1,3), C=(3,3). Under k=2, points move along OA,OB,OC to A′=(3,1),B′=(1,5),C′=(5,5). The triangle's side lengths are doubled and internal angles unchanged.

Teacher/student activity analogue: draw a nondegenerate polygon and its two dilations about the same centre, one at k=1/2 and one k=2; measure distances and lengths to a stated tolerance, record two ratio tables and critique any discrepancy caused by ruler uncertainty. Teacher rubric (0–4): correct centre and positive factor, accurate point placement, meaningful ratio table, and recognition of measurement error. Drawings and comparative observations are teacher assessed.
Source: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 3, CC BY 4.0. All diagrams are described verbally and all worked Edulytiks problems are independently authored.

KeyConcepts.Title: Centre-distance ratio
KeyConcepts.Definition: For dilation of P about O by factor k, OP′/OP=k whenever P≠O.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Multiply each nonzero distance from the centre by k.
KeyConcepts.Example: If OP=7 cm and k=3/2, OP′=10.5 cm.

KeyConcepts.Title: Corresponding segment ratio
KeyConcepts.Definition: Any corresponding nonzero segment length in a dilation is scaled by the same positive factor k.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use A′B′=k·AB for k>0; note a zero-length segment has no meaningful length ratio.
KeyConcepts.Example: If AB=6 cm and k=2/3, image length A′B′=4 cm.

KeyConcepts.Title: Measurement and error
KeyConcepts.Definition: A measured drawing may give approximate numerical ratios because physical marking has precision limits.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compare ratios within a stated tolerance and retain the exact mathematical relationship in the model.
KeyConcepts.Example: A measured 4.02 cm versus expected 4.00 cm is an approximation, not a new scale factor.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compute image centre distances
WorkedExamples.Question: O is dilation centre, OP=7 cm and k=3/2. Find OP′.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the definition of positive dilation.
Steps: Multiply the original radius: OP′=(3/2)·7=10.5 cm.
Place P′ on ray OP at 10.5 cm from O.
WorkedExamples.Check: For k>1 the image lies farther from O than P.

WorkedExamples.Title: Measure corresponding sides
WorkedExamples.Question: Original polygon side AB is 6 cm. A scale factor k=2/3 is applied. Find A′B′.
WorkedExamples.Method: Multiply the original segment length by k.
Steps: Image side is shorter, consistent with 0<k<1.
WorkedExamples.Check: Angles do not change, and the 2/3 ratio applies to all other nonzero corresponding sides.

WorkedExamples.Title: Coordinate dilation and pairwise lengths
WorkedExamples.Question: O=(1,1), A=(2,1), B=(1,3). Dilate by k=2 and compare AB with A′B′.
WorkedExamples.Method: Apply centre-vector rule and Pythagorean distance.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The side ratio is exactly 2, matching the dilation scale.
WorkedExamples.Check: The result comes from a consistent centre and factor, not independent rescaling of each vertex.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Computing a side ratio from a centre-point distance when that point equals the centre.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: OP=0 makes the quotient OP′/OP undefined.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use any point P≠O or a nonzero corresponding polygon side to measure the factor.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming measured discrepancies disprove the mathematical dilation theorem.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Ruler uncertainty affects drawings, not the exact theoretical construction.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Record measurement tolerance and verify exact proportions using coordinates or geometric reasoning.

SummaryPoints: Every nonzero centre-to-point distance is multiplied by k by definition.
All corresponding polygon segment lengths also scale by k; ratios require nonzero denominator.
A measurement investigation should distinguish exact model claims from finite-precision observations.
